n: After Babylon’s fall, the Lord will again show mercy to Israel, bring them back to their land, and foreigners will join them. This was partly fulfilled in the return from exile and points to the latter-day gathering.

f.w: the strangers shall be joined with them

n: Other nations will help bring Israel home, and the former captives will rule over their oppressors. 2 Nephi 24:2 adds “yea, from far unto the ends of the earth; and they shall return to their lands of promise,” widening it to a worldwide gathering.

f.g: Female servants.

n: When the Lord gives Israel rest from sorrow, fear, and hard slavery…
…they will sing a mocking song against the king of Babylon: “How the oppressor has stopped! The golden city is finished!”

f.g: Hebrew mashal — here a taunt-song.
Possibly “insolent fury”; the Hebrew word is uncertain.

n: The Lord has broken the club and scepter of wicked rulers.

f.g: A ruler’s staff, symbol of authority.

n: The tyrant who struck nations with endless blows and ruled in rage is now chased down himself, and no one comes to his rescue.

f.g: No one holds back his attackers.

n: With the tyrant gone, the whole earth rests in peace and bursts into song.
Even the trees celebrate! Since the king fell, no woodcutter comes to chop down Lebanon’s forests. Mesopotamian kings boasted of cutting cedars for their palaces.

f.g: Woodcutter.

n: The underworld is stirred to meet him. The ghosts of dead kings rise from their thrones to greet the newcomer.

f.g: Hebrew Sheol — the realm of the dead.
Literally “he-goats” — leaders of the flock.

n: They mock him: “So now you’re as weak as we are!” Death levels all human power.
His splendor and music have gone down to the grave. Maggots are his mattress and worms his blanket.

f.g: Harps or stringed instruments.

n: The famous lament: “How you have fallen from heaven, shining one, son of the dawn!” Though aimed at Babylon’s king, Latter-day Saints, with scripture, see here the fall of Satan, who rebelled in the premortal world.

f.g: Latin “light-bearer,” translating Hebrew helel — “shining one,” the morning star.

f.w: How art thou fallen from heaven

n: He said in his heart, “I will climb to heaven and set my throne above God’s stars, on the mountain where the gods assemble.” The repeated “I will” shows his pride.

f.g: The mountain of assembly — in ancient myths, where the gods met.
The far north, the legendary divine mountain.

n: “I will rise above the clouds; I will be like the Most High.” Lucifer sought God’s honor and power for himself.

f.w: I will be like the most High

n: Instead, he will be brought down to the depths of the pit. Pride leads to the lowest fall.

f.g: The deepest part of the grave or underworld.

n: People will stare at him and ask, “Is this the one who shook the earth and made kingdoms tremble?”

f.g: Stare intently.

n: “Is this the one who turned the world into a wasteland, destroyed cities, and never let his prisoners go home?”

f.w: opened not the house of his prisoners
f.g: Never released captives — Babylon held Judah captive.

n: Other kings rest in honor, each in his own grand tomb.
But this king is thrown out of his grave like a rejected branch, covered with the slain, trampled like a corpse. Being unburied was the ultimate disgrace.

f.g: A loathed, rejected shoot.

f.w: the raiment of those that are slain

n: He will not be buried with other kings, because he ruined his own land and killed his own people. His descendants will never be honored.
His sons will be killed for their fathers’ sins, so that they never rise to rule and fill the earth with cities again.
The Lord declares He will cut off Babylon’s name, survivors, and descendants.

f.g: Descendant, posterity.

n: Babylon will become a swamp for wild birds, swept away by God’s broom of destruction.

f.g: A marsh bird, or possibly a hedgehog.
A broom.

n: The Lord has sworn an oath: what He has planned will certainly happen.

f.w: as I have purposed, so shall it stand

n: He will crush Assyria in His own land and on His mountains. This happened when Sennacherib’s army was destroyed outside Jerusalem (701 BC). 2 Nephi 24:25 reads “bring the Assyrian.”
This is God’s plan for the whole earth, and His hand is stretched out over every nation.
Who can cancel what the Lord has decided? Who can turn back His outstretched hand? No one.

f.g: Cancel or annul.

n: This prophecy came in the year King Ahaz died, about 715 BC.
Don’t celebrate, Philistia, that the rod that struck you is broken. From the snake’s root will come a worse viper — a fiery, flying serpent. A new oppressor will rise.

f.g: Philistia, the coastal land of the Philistines.
A venomous snake.
Perhaps a swift, deadly snake; an image of a fierce enemy.

n: The poorest of God’s people will graze safely, but Philistia’s root will die by famine and its survivors be killed.

f.g: The poorest of the poor.

n: Wail, Philistine city gates! Smoke rises from the north — an invading army whose soldiers march in perfect order, no straggler among them.

f.g: Melted in fear.

f.w: none shall be alone in his appointed times
f.g: No soldier falls out of the ranks.

n: What answer should be given to foreign messengers? That the Lord has founded Zion, and His humble people will find refuge there. 2 Nephi 24 ends Nephi’s long Isaiah quotation here.
